display_name: Coast charted by Wilkes and later sailed through (segment to be identified)
what_was_reported: Continuous southern coast observed and charted over an extended run of longitude.
why_plausible: A long coast seen repeatedly over many days from a squadron of ships, in conditions where distant ice and distant land are hard to tell apart.
later_evidence: Later vessels sailed across positions charted as land.
notes: Deliberately carries no geometry. Which segment, at what position, on which sheet is unknown (ant-gap-wilkes-sheets), and drawing a line for a disproof we cannot locate would repeat the original error in our own voice. current_scholarly_status stays unresolved because much of Wilkes's coast was correct.

what_was_reported: An extensive coast reported in the Weddell Sea, running south from around 62 degrees south, described with landmarks and soundings.
why_plausible: Morrell was sailing in the same exceptional ice year that let Weddell reach an extraordinary latitude, in a sea that was demonstrably open that season and closed in most others. A coast reported from there in 1823 was not absurd on its face.
later_evidence: Later voyages, including the Endurance drift across much of the same water, found open sea and pack where the coast was placed.
notes: The programme's strongest ghost case after Wilkes, and the one that connects Act VI directly to Act VIII: Endurance drifted through the water Morrell had charted as land. Morrell's reliability is separately disputed in the literature, which is a question about the man and not about the feature, and the two are kept apart. No cause is attributed.

what_was_reported: A range reported to the south of the Ross Sea coast and named after Ross's former commander.
why_plausible: Ross was an experienced observer working in clear polar air, where distance and elevation are notoriously hard to judge and where a far snowfield can read as a nearer range.
later_evidence: Later parties working over the same ground did not find a range as charted.
notes: Included because the claimant is the most reliable observer in the dataset. A ghost feature attributable to a careless witness teaches nothing; one attributable to Ross is the whole argument of Act VI. The plausibility note stops short of naming refraction as the cause, because no source is held for that.

what_was_reported: An island reported in the far South Pacific, with a described position, subsequently repeated on charts and searched for by later vessels.
why_plausible: A single reported position in an ocean nobody crossed often, in an era when a chart had no way to record that a feature rested on one unconfirmed report.
later_evidence: Reported to have been searched for without result and eventually removed from charts. No authority for the removal is held here.
notes: A sub-Antarctic phantom rather than a continental one, kept because it is the clearest case of the pattern the reusable methodology is for: report, repetition, search, removal. Filed as unresolved rather than disproved: the removal is reported but no authority for it is held, and the validator refuses a disproof that cannot name what disproved it. Ramsay is a popular survey and the audit has already ruled that it may not carry an individual case.

what_was_reported: An island reported south of New Zealand and carried on charts for over a century.
why_plausible: The southern ocean between Australasia and the ice was crossed rarely and charted from scattered reports, so a single sighting had little against it.
later_evidence: Reported to have been searched for without result and eventually removed from charts. No authority for the removal is held here.
notes: The same pattern as Dougherty and worth holding beside it, because two independent phantoms in the same waters say something about the waters rather than about the observers. Filed as unresolved rather than disproved: the removal is reported but no authority for it is held, and the validator refuses a disproof that cannot name what disproved it.
